en: Before the inexorable hero Tengir,
He brought in his nobles,
The golden throne of Kakan,
He seated him upon it in ceremony,
Posting guards, they rested quietly,
Again taking tribute and appraisers,
Taking the enemy who had encircled and listened,
Guarding their sight, taking the mountain,
With an uproar that split the earth,
Such was the khan’s might,
Crossing ridge after ridge,
Crossing the lofty Aksa mountain,
Inflicting this suffering,
Driving the scattered deer before them,
Binding tigers upon the ridge,
Spreading his road-guard out,
It was the time he set the pacers moving,
Ruining all whom he encountered,
It was the time he cast them into the enclosure.
Many souls traveled between,
When he came to confront them,
If you perceive the calamity,
Now when he came forward,
Chyngteñir poured out his wrath,
He scattered a dragon’s venom,
Wearying horses and scouting the land,
Rousing the people and taking the day,
Taking every covered garden,
He brought disaster upon them,
Bursting forth from the mountain,
His eyes struck like lightning,
Taking away two old men,
Subduing the world,
Again he came to know his people.
The enemy became blood,
All the Kyrgyz learned it together.
When he saw it from the valley,
Leaving the world in grief,
He reached those who confronted him.
The champion’s great fortress,
He saw its blessing.
If one ruined paradise,
If the champion had an enemy,
He brought true death upon him.
He turned the encountered enemy to ash,
He destroyed whoever came against him,
His bitter wrath scattered,
Again it swelled violently,
Any soul who came before him,
Became one of his people.
Putting the unruly in their places,
Massing the wrathful host,
Contending against a thousand men,
Breaking through with the army,
He faced toward the sunset.
Its brushed side became like fire,
Despairing of the life caught in peril,
It brought grievous hardship upon them.
Drawing back his speech, he held to the faith,
Taking the lead before the people,
He made Dombai’s land rise in dust,
When they struggled, he fixed his gaze,
Making a dwelling where he saw a fit place,
He ruled the side that rode out,
His expedition became countless and vast,
His temples showed outward, swollen,
They dug defenses and halted there.
Billowing as though fire had swept over it,
Oh Tengir, what grievous hardship!
It became evident to every soul.
His army formed a surrounding host.
In his great host there were champions,
Those who saw them fell into grievous distress.
The reason for their lament was this:
That hero Chyngteñir,
Whose watching wrath was fierce,
From the multitude that could shatter forty,
A prodigy sprung from a wild boar,
His rage could tear hell apart,
No man sent against him returned,
Even the black-headed stag stood amazed,
He allowed no equal to challenge him,
In the eighteen thousand worlds,
No such courage had been heard of,
Among heroes, he was the foremost,
He was champion and khan alike,
He was the chosen one of fourfold strength.
He was khan of the countless Chinese,
A soul greater than so many others,
The hero above all men.
When he drank blood, he was never sated,
Countless myriads of troops did not daunt him,
When blades clashed, none could reach him,
No man could match his force.
In the span of his own life,
The world had brought forth no equal.
At his birth, as the tale tells,
The earth shook and awakened,
Saying, “He truly is Tengir,”
He was given a mighty name.
To that hero Chyngteñir,
What mortal sent could approach?
Who could gird himself and fight him alone?
Was any such place left in all the world?
Such was Chyngteñir’s nature,
The sun set at the sight of his power,
Forty cried out as lives fell,
The people scattered as bodies lay,
He became a star over the world.
Rising past the dawn and glowing,
Shimmering at the mouth of dawn,
The birches’ crowns whistled,
The branches at dawn bent low,
The face of the sun was outlined,
The fierce men clad in armor,
Those who went armored in stone,
Holding sway over a thousand households,
The khan’s valiant heralds,
Came out in ranks,
Before great Tengir,
Bowing low in homage,
The leaders of the people stood proud,
His narrowed eyes flashing fiercely,
He never abandoned his greed,
When he spoke to the accursed one,
He unfolded the words that had befallen them,
Each time one died, they multiplied,
Fortune itself followed him,
The formidable Kyrgyz lineage,
The fallen Kyrgyz, fellow people of the land,
To his command and his word,
Tell Jeljetpes that they must submit,
Their treasure and daughter to Tengir,
Tell Jaljetpes they must give,
I continued from what was handed down,
I asked those who knew,
I did not stray from the truth-tellers,
I did not take from embellishments.
I will not let them range freely and reap,
I will not let his people sow grain,
I will not let his people summer in the mountains,
Kenen’s daughter Kermekash,
Your poor beauty, fairer than one behind a screen,
Dress her in a ring-mail coat,
Mount her upon Kertulpar,
Tell her to ride the moon-swift racer,
Without being deprived of games and gatherings,
A lifeless man will deliver her,
Taking four iron hands,
Stretching around, he will carry her away,
A man left sprawling will be a pitiful sight,
A thousand arrows will be like white frost,
Tell him to submit to the words spoken.
When Chyngteñir mounts and stands ready,
Across the whole moonlit world,
To rule as sovereign,
Tell them to surrender every villain.
If he starts trouble from the outset,
Tell him Kermekash must remain in the land.
He who turned back the black night,
Who spoke eloquently before the people,
A master of words about prosperity,
He was a broad-hearted hero,
I am Chyng, the Great Tengir,
Giving this command to you,
Hear clearly the words I speak.
For the khan to take what is due,
Let a thousand tracts remain and let him yield his share,
To surrender the daughters to Chyng,
Let him bow his neck as far as required,
Let him pay levy and tribute in money,
Let him give gold and treasure by the pud,
Let him give ten thousand remount horses,
If he scowls and sets himself in defiance,
Such is the khan’s dominion,
Let no Kalmak speak against it.
This is the padishah’s dominion,
Let him quickly submit to the profitable word spoken,
Let him promptly give what the envoys demand.
If he does not heed my worthy words,
Every proper remedy will be exhausted,
The people will be slaughtered and scattered,
Across the ridges, alas,
Let him not expose them to ruin.
Women and young children alike,
Great and small, old and young,
Women and men together,
Their land and resolve will be conquered,
They met with Jetpes,
Let no blood-guilt remain upon them.
Let every girded man return without exception,
Bring back the message itself,
O sons of the white-kalpak Kyrgyz,
The knot at the heart of profound words,
The sovereign who bound them all together,
At their head, this pure one,
The deep pool of a flowing river,
The great man of the white-capped people,
You shall withdraw from his side,
If he places hope in his livestock,
Tell him to submit to the words thus spoken.
Without stirring up a quarrel,
Without shouting or slaughtering one another,
Without arguing or fighting,
Without resisting even the lesser levy,
Without making such a commotion,
Tell him therefore to submit to the spoken word.
Without deviating a hair from that command,
Tell him to give it to Khan Tengir.
Tell him he will see a mighty conflict.
Let him rage if an army comes,
Upon the pass at his waist,
While the warrior is in your hands,
Let skill reach his neck,
Let him not think himself our equal,
Blood broth will spill into his breast,
What else but ruin will befall him?
Certain death will come upon him,
There are many words to go on speaking,
The words are exhausted; the matter is settled.
The dawn of words spoken truly,
The foremost of the renowned lions,
With five days as the appointed time.
I have fallen in love with Zhalzhal,
Come and soothe my burning heart.
Do not fear; come with your eyes open.
If you prove equal to what I have said,
For the sake of the light, Zhelzhetpes,
I will defend the word that was spoken,
I will give you whatever you desire.
I will send word to the people,
I will bless the people of the forty khans,
As one khan among them, you,
I will raise and acclaim as khan.
Among the black Kalmyks and Manchus,
I will have you rule among them,
If you prove worthy of the words spoken,
I will place a golden crown upon you.
I will make this Beijing acknowledge you,
I will settle in Beijing,
Its two daughters and one true one,
Let Zhelzhetpes keep coming.
The assembly of the khagan's people,
Zhelzhetpes became a great lord,
Saying the hero had risen above the rest,
Saying Zhelzhetpes had become a pasha,
The people stirred among themselves.
As he stood speaking his words,
As he fully explained himself,
Of the mighty Padishah Tengir,
Saying all his deeds were pure,
Calling him a sovereign surpassing the world,
“All my wishes have come,” he said,
“What I desired has been granted,” he said,
“My ruined affair has been set right,”
“My flown bird has alighted,” he said,
